source.title: MINIMAX APPROXIMATION AS A METHOD FOR OVERCOMING THE DOUBLE DESCENT PHENOMENON

record.file_problem: none; the text contains the full paper, including its conclusions and references.
record.tranche_reason: The paper makes qualitative claims about controlling model complexity and identifying a second-descent point, but gives no experimental protocol or quantitative measurements to establish the model-size curve.
record.gate_note: The paper states that minimax approximation identifies a second-descent point and that increasing parameter count with control of maximum losses can improve generalization. It provides no model names, dataset, parameter counts, numerical results, or supporting figures or tables. The comparison with early stopping and dropout is mentioned without results and is not recorded as a row. The L1/L2 test-loss claim is recorded under fits_no_version because it does not measure whether regularization removes or changes a double-descent peak.
record.test_reason: This is a short conference paper that takes double descent as given and proposes minimax approximation to overcome it. It reports no models, datasets, parameter counts, metrics or numbers. It gives only qualitative claims about its own method, such as finding the second-descent point and beating early stopping and dropout. It never measures a test-error curve over model size, epochs or samples. It concerns mitigation without reporting how often or how strongly the behaviour appears, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that minimax approximation is a powerful tool for overcoming double descent. They say it controls model complexity and worst-case losses, reduces overfitting, optimizes parameter count, and stabilizes test results. They add that it works better combined with L1/L2 regularization and is not universal, so it should be paired with cross-validation and adaptive learning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes minimax approximation with regularization, rather than reproducing the methods or measurements of the cited double-descent studies.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper asserts that minimax approximation (minimizing maximum loss) reduces overfitting, finds the second-descent point, and beats early stopping and dropout on test data. No numbers are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimax (worst-case) loss minimization mitigates double descent and improves test performance relative to early stopping and dropout.

fits_no_version.finding: The paper asserts that combining L1/L2 regularization with minimax reduced test loss and improved robustness. No metric or values are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Combining minimax approximation with L1/L2 regularization reduces test loss.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of XVII International Conference Measurement and Control in Complex System (MCCS-2024); peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The text gives qualitative conclusions without specifying models, datasets, procedures, metrics, numerical outcomes, uncertainty, or supporting tables and figures.
record.rows_left_out: The stated comparison with early stopping and dropout has no reported outcome or values and is omitted. No additional reported results bear on the tested claim versions.

untested.parts: The test-error curve over model size, the peak near the interpolation threshold, and any measured model are all not tested.
Mentions L1/L2 regularization and noisy data, but does not measure how either changes the double-descent peak.

record.verdict_notes: The paper contains no experimental evidence and only three references, one of them Belkin et al., an original source. Its introduction also mischaracterizes double descent as degradation from overfitting. The record's fits_no_version entry pointed to a non-existent row r2; this has been corrected. The relation and tranche were changed from tests/T2 to uses_without_test/T4, and the V1 limits_scope label was removed, because no result bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not provide the fall-rise-fall curve over model size, identify an interpolation threshold, or give model-specific measurements.
The paper mentions L1/L2 regularization and lower test losses, but does not test how regularization or noise affects the double-descent peak.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.size_stated: models with a large number of parameters; parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Gradually increase the number of model parameters while controlling maximum losses.
rows.measure: Generalization and the point of second descent; specific test metric not stated.
rows.value: The text says the approach can improve generalization and helped identify the point where results improved again after overfitting.
rows.locator: Results section: model-complexity optimization and optimal point of second descent
rows.note: Qualitative assertion only; the text does not show the full curve or establish that the point is near the size that just fits the training set.
rows.check: This is not a measurement of the model-wise curve. It is an unsupported qualitative claim about the paper's own minimax method improving generalization and locating the second descent. There is no subject, baseline, metric or value, so 'partial' cannot be read from it. If kept at all, it belongs under fits_no_version or should be dropped as an own-method performance claim.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Qualitative claim about increasing parameter count under minimax approximation
reader_labels.reason: The paper asserts that results improve again after overfitting, but does not show the full model-size curve or locate the peak relative to interpolation (r1).
